blocks.text: Two databases with the same API can behave completely differently under load because of how they lay data out on disk. Write-heavy event streams, read-heavy relational lookups and analytical scans each favour a different engine. Knowing B-trees, LSM-trees and columnar layouts lets you justify choices like "Cassandra for messages, Postgres for accounts, ClickHouse for analytics".

A B-tree stores sorted keys in fixed-size pages (typically 8–16 KB) arranged as a shallow, wide tree. A lookup reads one page per level — 3 or 4 pages for billions of rows, most of them cached. Writes find the leaf page and modify it in place; if the page is full it splits. To survive crashes mid-update, every change is first appended to the write-ahead log.

items: Strengths: predictable reads, efficient range scans, mature transactional engines (Postgres, MySQL InnoDB, SQL Server).
Weaknesses: random I/O for writes, page splits and fragmentation, write amplification (WAL + page writes).

steps.label: flush when full → new immutable SSTable

items: Strengths: very high write throughput (sequential I/O only), good compression, natural for time-ordered and append-heavy data (Cassandra, RocksDB, ScyllaDB, LevelDB, Bigtable).
Weaknesses: reads may consult several files; compaction consumes I/O and can cause latency spikes; deletes are tombstones.

cols.title: Size-tiered
pros: Low write amplification; good for write-heavy loads
cons: More SSTables per read; temporary 2× disk during compaction

cols.title: Leveled
pros: Each level has non-overlapping key ranges → fewer files per read

cols.title: Time-window
pros: Great for TTL'd time-series: whole files expire

items: An analytical query (`SUM(amount) WHERE country = 'IN'`) reads only two columns instead of whole rows.
Similar values sit together, so compression (dictionary, run-length, delta) is excellent — often 5–10×.
Engines process column chunks with vectorised (SIMD) execution.
Formats and engines: Parquet, ORC, ClickHouse, BigQuery, Snowflake, Redshift, Druid, Pinot.

blocks.text: Time-series databases (Prometheus TSDB, InfluxDB, TimescaleDB) combine ideas: an in-memory head block with a WAL (LSM-like), immutable compressed blocks per time range, columnar-style compression of timestamps (delta-of-delta) and values (XOR, Gorilla), and retention by dropping whole blocks.

blocks.title: Say it in the interview
blocks.text: Messages are append-heavy and read by (channel, time), so an LSM-based wide-column store fits; account balances need transactions, so they stay in Postgres; analytics go to a columnar warehouse fed by CDC.
